questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={x}^{2}-6x$ at the point $(3,-9).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{2}-6x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-6x)=2x-6.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(3)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3)=2(3)-6=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=0$ and the coordinates of our point $(3,-9),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-9) & =0(x-3) \\ y & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{16}{x}^{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{16}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{16}\cdot 4{x}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(2)$, which gives

$$
{f}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{4}\cdot {2}^{3}=2.
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=2$ and the coordinates of our point $(2,1),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =2(x-2) \\ y & =2x-4+1 \\ y & =2x-3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y={x}^{2}+5x$ at the point $(-1,-4).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{2}+5x.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+5x)=2x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(-1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1)=2(-1)+5=3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=3$ and the coordinates of our point $(-1,-4),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-4) & =3(x-(-1)) \\ y+4 & =3(x+1) \\ y & =3x+3-4 \\ y & =3x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find where the tangent to the curve  $y=\frac{5}{x}-2x$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{5}{x}-2x.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{5}{x}-2x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5{x}^{-1}-2x) \\  & =-5{x}^{-2}-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-5(1)^{-2}-2=-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(3) & =-7(x-1) \\ y & =-7x+7+3 \\ y & =-7x+10.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $x=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-7(0)+10 \\ y & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(0,10).$

Find where the tangent to the curve $y={x}^{3}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}$ at the point  $(-1,-2)$ intersects the $y$-axis.

questions.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{3}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}-{x}^{-2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-2}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-(-2{x}^{-3}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
\begin{aligned}m & ={f}^{′}(-1) \\  & =3(-1)^{2}+\frac{2}{(-1)^{3}} \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =1\cdot [x-(-1)] \\ y+2 & =x+1 \\ y & =x+1-2 \\ y & =x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $y$-axis, we set $x=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =0-1 \\ y & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(0,-1).$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y = 2x^3 - 2x$ at the point $(1,0).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $f(x) = 2x^3 - 2x.$ Computing the derivative $f'(x)$ gives

$$
f'(x)  = 6x^2-2.
$$

We then compute $f'(1)$, which gives

$$
f'(1)  = 6(1)^2-2 = 4.
$$

Finally, we use the point-slope form with $m=4$ and the coordinates of our point $(1,0),$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =4(x-1) \\ y & =4x-4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find where the tangent to the curve $y=4\sqrt{x}+4x$ at the point $(1,8)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=4\sqrt{x}+4x.$ Let's first calculate the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4\sqrt{x}+4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{1/2}+4x) \\  & =2{x}^{-1/2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the slope of the tangent at our point is

$$
m=f'(1) = 2(1)^{-1/2}+4 = 6.
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-8 & =6(x-1) \\ y & =6x-6+8 \\ y & =6x+2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find where the tangent line intercepts the $x$-axis, we set $y=0$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =6x+2 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point of intersection is $\left(-\dfrac 1 3, 0\right).$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The equation of the tangent line to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $P(x_1,y_1),$ in point-slope form, is given by

$$
y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{.75cm} m=f'(x_1).
$$

Here, $m = f'(x_1)$ because $f'(x_1)$ represents the slope of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at the point $(x_1,y_1).$

For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the tangent line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $P(1,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14212785/assets/487d21289b468fb82efa2097e425dd560811dc3165890509dacbab8093e0ecdb.png)

Since $y=x^2,$ we have $f(x)=x^2.$ We begin by calculating the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) 		 = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x
$$

Then, we determine the slope of the tangent at $P(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
m = f'(1)  = 2(1) = 2
$$

 

Finally, we substitute the slope $m=2$ and the coordinates of $P(1,1)$ into the point-slope form, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =2(x-1) \\ y & =2x-2+1 \\ y & =2x-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the tangent is $y=2x-1.$
